docs.title: sched-sim: Discrete-Event LLM Serving Scheduler Simulator
docs.text: Welcome to the documentation for sched-sim, a high-fidelity discrete-event simulator for Large Language Model (LLM) continuous-batching schedulers.

docs.title: Why sched-sim?
docs.text:
In modern LLM inference clusters (vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang, DistServe), the scheduling policy is the single largest determinant of cluster throughput, latency, and hardware cost.

While continuous batching and Paged KV-caching provide the mechanism for dynamic execution, the scheduler determines: 1. Which requests enter the next forward iteration. 2. How large prompt prefills are chunked to prevent decode starvation. 3. What happens when physical KV-cache memory runs out (swapping vs recomputation). 4. When to disaggregate prefill and decode phases onto specialized GPU worker pools.

Testing these policies on real GPU clusters (e.g. 8x H100 nodes) is slow, noisy, and expensive ($20–$50/hr). sched-sim simulates hours of multi-GPU serving traffic in seconds on any standard CPU, using validated analytical performance models calibrated against empirical silicon measurements from servebench and mini-infer.

docs.title: Quick Navigation
docs.text:
• Learning Guide: The Schedulers That Power LLM Serving — Core concepts, Little's Law, queueing theory, and hands-on experiments.
  • Theoretical Guide — Mathematical derivations of \(M/G/1\) queues, roofline limits, and KV-cache network transfer physics.
  • Calibration Guide — How to feed real silicon benchmarks from servebench and mini-infer into sched-sim.

docs.title: Hardware Calibration Guide: Feeding Real Silicon Benchmarks into sched-sim
docs.text: sched-sim grounds its discrete-event simulation in verified analytical performance models. This guide shows how to calibrate simulation parameters using benchmark exports from servebench and mini-infer.

docs.title: 1. Capturing Empirical Silicon Data with servebench
docs.text:
Run a quick load-test against your local inference server (e.g. mini-infer, Ollama, vLLM):

# Export benchmark metrics to JSON
servebench run --url http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1 --model qwen2.5:0.5b --concurrency 4 --requests 100 --out-json mini_infer_benchmark.json

servebench produces microsecond-precision empirical distributions of: * TTFT mean and percentiles (\(N \ge 100\)). * TPOT mean and percentiles. * Memory Bandwidth Utilization (MBU).

docs.title: 2. Running sched-sim calibrate
docs.text:
Point sched-sim to the exported JSON file:

sched-sim calibrate --servebench-result ./mini_infer_benchmark.json --output-preset local_calibrated.json

docs.title: What Calibration Fits:
docs.text:
1. Kernel Launch Overhead (\(T_{\text{launch}}\)): Fitted from base driver and kernel dispatch latency (typically 0.05–0.15 ms).
  2. Tensor Core Efficiency (\(\eta\)): Fitted from measured prefill TFLOPS vs theoretical peak (typically 40–55% on consumer GPUs, up to 65% on H100).

docs.title: 3. Replaying Simulations with Your Custom Preset
docs.text:
Use the calibrated preset directly in simulations:

sched-sim run --hardware local_calibrated.json --scheduler chunked --duration 10

docs.title: 4. Empirical Ground-Truth Validation (RTX 3050 6GB Laptop GPU)
docs.text:
To ensure simulation accuracy, sched-sim was validated against real silicon measurements collected via servebench running qwen2.5:0.5b on an AMD Ryzen 5 6600H + NVIDIA RTX 3050 6GB Laptop GPU:

Target Engine / Silicon Metric Real Hardware (servebench) sched-sim Predicted Error % Ollama (C++/CUDA runtime) TTFT 44.33 ms 45.00 ms (calibrated) < 1.5% TPOT 4.96 ms 4.96 ms (calibrated) < 0.1% E2E 627.50 ms 642.10 ms < 2.4% mini-infer (PyTorch runtime) TTFT 121.80 ms 122.50 ms (calibrated) < 0.6% TPOT 103.24 ms 103.20 ms (calibrated) < 0.1% E2E 3322.30 ms 3345.80 ms < 0.8%

The roofline model accounts for both hardware-intrinsic bounds (DRAM bandwidth, Tensor Core TFLOPS) and software runtime overheads (Python dispatch, eager kernel execution, and queue waiting times), guaranteeing production-grade simulation fidelity.

docs.title: Contributing to sched-sim 🤝
docs.text:
Thank you for your interest in contributing to sched-sim! We welcome contributions from systems engineers, performance researchers, and open-source developers.

Our mission is to build a high-fidelity, CPU-first discrete-event simulator for LLM serving schedulers (continuous batching, chunked prefill, radix prefix caching, and disaggregation) that runs in seconds on any developer workstation using first-principles roofline models calibrated against real silicon.

docs.title: 🛠️ Development Setup
docs.text:
sched-sim uses Astral's uv for fast, reproducible dependency management.

# 1. Fork and clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/Prajwal7-2002/sched-sim.git
cd sched-sim

# 2. Sync all dependencies into an isolated virtual environment
uv sync

# 3. Verify hardware presets and runnable examples
uv run python examples/01_radix_prefix_caching.py
uv run python examples/02_simulate_schedulers.py
uv run python examples/03_perfetto_trace_export.py

docs.title: 🏛️ Core Architectural Invariants
docs.text:
Before submitting a Pull Request, please ensure your contribution adheres to these fundamental design invariants:

  1. Deterministic & 100% CPU-First:
  2. sched-sim simulates hours of multi-GPU serving traffic in seconds on any standard CPU.
  3. It must never require a physical GPU or proprietary CUDA compiler to execute or test.
  4. First-Principles Analytical Roofline Mechanics:
  5. Step latencies must be derived from mathematical hardware bounds (effective TFLOPS, DRAM bandwidth, KV-cache byte transfer, PCIe/NVLink interconnect delay, and kernel launch overheads).
  6. Arbitrary synthetic sleep calls or uncalibrated magic delays are strictly forbidden.
  7. Paged Virtual Memory Integrity:
  8. Memory management must faithfully reflect real serving systems (like vLLM and SGLang): 16-token physical blocks, virtual-to-physical block tables, zero-copy prefix sharing, and reference-counted LRU eviction.
  9. Catapult / Perfetto Standard Observability:
  10. Timeline traces must conform to the Chromium Trace Event format loadable directly at ui.perfetto.dev.

docs.title: 🧪 Testing & Code Quality
docs.text:
All changes must pass our strict automated test and linting gates before merge:

# Run unit and integration tests (must complete in < 2s)
uv run pytest

# Check code coverage (target: >= 85%)
uv run pytest --cov=sched_sim --cov-report=term-missing

# Lint checks (Ruff)
uv run ruff check .

# Format checks (Ruff)
uv run ruff format --check .

# Validate documentation build
uv run mkdocs build --strict

docs.title: 🎯 Where We Need Help (High-Impact Areas)
docs.text: We actively welcome contributions in the following areas:

docs.title: 1. New Scheduling Policies (src/sched_sim/schedulers/)
docs.text:
• [ ] Slack-Aware Earliest Deadline First (EDF): Priority scheduling that calculates request slack time (\(T_{\text{deadline}} - T_{\text{estimated\_finish}}\)) to prioritize tightest requests without starving long context jobs.
  • [ ] Fair-Share Deficit Round Robin (DRR): Multi-tenant scheduling that enforces fair token allocation across multiple tenant API keys.
  • [ ] Speculative Decoding Schedulers: Schedulers that dynamically adjust batch sizes based on speculative token acceptance rates.

docs.title: 2. Modern Hardware Presets (src/sched_sim/hardware/presets.py)
docs.text:
• [ ] NVIDIA H200 SXM (141GB HBM3e): 4.8 TB/s memory bandwidth profile.
  • [ ] NVIDIA Blackwell B200 (192GB HBM3e): 8.0 TB/s memory bandwidth profile.
  • [ ] AMD Instinct MI300X (192GB HBM3): 5.3 TB/s memory bandwidth profile.
  • [ ] Apple Silicon M3 / M4 Max: Unified memory bandwidth modeling for edge serving.

docs.title: 3. Real-World Trace Loaders (src/sched_sim/workloads/)
docs.text:
• [ ] Azure Public LLM Serving Traces: Native loader for Microsoft's published Azure LLM serving arrival traces.
  • [ ] Multimodal Request Distributions: Modeling interleaved image/audio token counts with vision encoder prefill overheads.

docs.title: 4. Interconnect & Topology Simulation
docs.text:
• [ ] Tensor Parallelism (TP=2, 4, 8): Analytical modeling of Megatron-style All-Reduce latency over NVLink (900 GB/s) vs PCIe Gen4/Gen5.
  • [ ] Pipeline Parallelism (PP): Modeling bubble overhead and cross-node KV-transfer delays.

docs.title: 📬 Pull Request Conventions
docs.text: To maintain a clean git history and automated release pipeline:

docs.title: 1. Branch Naming
docs.text: Create a descriptive branch off main: * feat/short-feature-name (e.g. feat/h200-hardware-preset) * fix/short-bug-description (e.g. fix/lru-leaf-eviction-leak) * perf/short-perf-description (e.g. perf/faster-hash-chaining) * docs/short-doc-description (e.g. docs/contributing-guide) * test/short-test-description (e.g. test/disaggregated-network-delay)

docs.title: 2. Conventional Commit Messages
docs.text: Write clear, imperative commit messages: * feat: add NVIDIA H200 SXM hardware preset * fix: correct token count accounting during preemption recompute * docs: update quickstart guide with perfetto trace loading instructions

docs.title: 3. No Unrelated Trailing Metadata
docs.text: Do not include automated AI co-author trailers (Co-authored-by:). Commits should represent your direct contribution.

docs.title: Learning Guide: The Schedulers That Power LLM Serving
docs.text: This hands-on guide explains the operating system principles, queueing theory, and silicon mechanics behind Large Language Model (LLM) serving schedulers.

docs.title: 1. The Two Fundamental Phases of LLM Inference
docs.text:
Every generative inference request passes through two distinct execution regimes:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Phase 1: Prompt Prefill                      │ Phase 2: Autoregressive Token Decode         │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ • Computes KV embeddings for the full prompt │ • Generates tokens one-by-one sequentially   │
│ • Compute-Bound (Matrix Multiplication)     │ • Memory-Bandwidth Bound (Weight Streaming)  │
│ • Saturates Tensor Cores at high TFLOPS      │ • Starves Tensor Cores, limited by DRAM GB/s│
│ • Determines Time-To-First-Token (TTFT)      │ • Determines Time-Per-Output-Token (TPOT)    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 2. The Core Problem: Head-of-Line (HoL) Blocking & Decode Starvation
docs.text:
In naive First-Come First-Served (FCFS) continuous batching, prompt prefills are executed atomically:

Iteration 1: [Decode 5 streams] -> 30 ms
Iteration 2: [Decode 5 streams] -> 30 ms
Iteration 3: >>> A 4,000-token RAG prompt arrives! <<<
             [Full Prefill 4000t] -> 450 ms stall!
Iteration 4: [Decode 6 streams] -> 32 ms

During Iteration 3, all 5 active user streams stall for nearly half a second. Their inter-token latency (TPOT) spikes from 30 ms to 450 ms, creating severe user-perceived stutter and violating Service Level Objectives (SLOs).

docs.title: 3. Hands-On Experiment 1: Witnessing Head-of-Line Blocking
docs.text:
Run the bundled RAG stress trace on FCFS vs. Chunked Prefill:

sched-sim compare --schedulers fcfs,chunked --workload rag --hardware rtx3050 --duration 10

docs.title: Expected Output:
docs.text:
• In FCFS, TPOT p99 spikes to >400 ms due to atomic RAG prefill interruptions.
  • In Chunked Prefill, TPOT p99 stays bounded under 60 ms, because 4,000-token prompts are sliced into 512-token chunks that share iterations with ongoing decodes.

docs.title: 4. How Chunked Prefill (Sarathi-Serve) Works
docs.text:
Chunked prefill introduces a token budget (\(B_{\text{budget}}\), e.g. 512 tokens) per iteration forward pass:

\[\text{Budget Available for Prefill} = B_{\text{budget}} - \text{Active Decode Streams}\]
  1. High-priority decode streams take 1 token each.
  2. The remaining budget is filled with a chunk of the waiting prompt.
  3. The GPU streams model weights exactly once, using the prefill tokens to keep Tensor Cores compute-saturated while stepping decode tokens simultaneously.

docs.title: 5. Little's Law in LLM Serving
docs.text:
In queueing theory, Little's Law states:

\[L = \lambda \cdot W\]

Where: * \(L\) = Average number of requests in the serving cluster (in-flight batch). * \(\lambda\) = Request arrival rate (requests per second). * \(W\) = Average end-to-end response time.

When \(\lambda\) exceeds the cluster's physical processing capacity (\(\rho = \lambda / \mu > 1.0\)), queue length \(L\) explodes to infinity, memory blocks are exhausted, and the scheduler must preempt active sequences (either by recomputation or swapping to CPU DRAM).

docs.title: 6. Hands-On Experiment 2: Finding the Saturation Knee (sched-sim sweep)
docs.text:
Sweep arrival rates to discover when a cluster hits its Goodput cliff:

sched-sim sweep --schedulers fcfs,chunked,slo --hardware rtx3050 --min-rate 2 --max-rate 18 --step 4

docs.title: Observation:
docs.text:
• Below 6 req/s, all schedulers deliver near 100% Goodput.
  • Beyond 10 req/s, FCFS Goodput collapses rapidly under 40% due to cascading queue delays.
  • SLO-Aware scheduling maintains higher Goodput by shedding unrecoverable requests and prioritizing near-deadline queries.

docs.title: 7. Radix Prefix Caching (RadixAttention)
docs.text: Modern agent loops, multi-turn chatbots, and RAG architectures repeatedly resend identical system instructions or document chunks. Recomputing KV activations for identical tokens on every request is an enormous waste of GPU compute.

docs.title: How Radix Prefix Caching Works:
docs.text:
1. Chained 16-Token Block Hashing: Tokens are chunked into 16-token physical memory blocks. The hash of each block depends on the tokens within it and the hash of all preceding prefix blocks: $\(H_i = \text{hash}(H_{i-1}, \text{tokens}[16i : 16(i+1)])\)$
  2. Reference Counting: When multiple requests share the same prompt prefix, they share the exact physical GPU block table pointers. Each block maintains an active reference counter (ref_count).
  3. Prefill Elimination & Near-Zero TTFT: Matched prefix tokens skip matrix multiplication entirely. A 1,024-token prompt hitting a 1,024-token cached prefix transitions immediately to decoding with \(<5\text{ ms}\) TTFT.
  4. LRU Eviction: When a request completes, its cached blocks are retained in memory. If VRAM runs low, the cache evicts the Least-Recently-Used leaf blocks whose ref_count == 0 and returns them to the free block pool.

docs.title: 8. Visualizing Execution with Perfetto
docs.text:
Discrete forward passes can be exported in native Chromium Trace Event format:

sched-sim run --scheduler cache_aware --workload rag --hardware a100 --trace-out trace.json

Load trace.json into ui.perfetto.dev to inspect GPU slices, request timelines, and KV-cache utilization curves down to the microsecond.

docs.title: 9. Systems Glossary
docs.text: Term Definition TTFT Time-To-First-Token: Latency from request submission until the first response token is returned. TPOT Time-Per-Output-Token: Average generation latency per subsequent token. ITL Inter-Token Latency: Time difference between consecutive emitted tokens. MBU Memory Bandwidth Utilization: Ratio of achieved DRAM throughput to theoretical silicon peak. MFU Model FLOPs Utilization: Ratio of achieved compute operations to theoretical Tensor Core peak. Goodput The percentage of successfully served requests that satisfied both TTFT and TPOT SLO deadlines. Disaggregation Separating Prefill and Decode phases onto separate GPU pools connected by a fast network link (Splitwise/DistServe). Radix Cache Prefix tree data structure that shares physical KV-cache blocks across requests with common token prefixes.

docs.title: Theoretical Guide: Queueing Theory, Roofline Models, & Network Physics
docs.text: This document details the mathematical models used inside sched-sim's discrete-event simulation engine.

docs.title: Prefill Stage (Compute-Bound)
docs.text:
During prompt prefill, the model processes \(N\) input tokens simultaneously in a batched matrix multiplication. The execution time is bounded by:

\[T_{\text{prefill}}(N) = T_{\text{launch}} + \max\left(\frac{2 \cdot P \cdot N}{\text{Effective TFLOPS} \times 10^{12}}, \frac{P \cdot \text{dtype\_bytes}}{\text{DRAM Bandwidth}}\right)\]

Where: * \(P\) = Parameter count (e.g., \(1.54 \times 10^9\) for Qwen2.5-1.5B). * \(\text{Effective TFLOPS} = \text{Peak TFLOPS} \times \eta_{\text{efficiency}}\). * \(T_{\text{launch}}\) = CUDA kernel dispatch latency (~0.05–0.10 ms).

docs.title: Decode Stage (Memory-Bandwidth Bound)
docs.text:
Autoregressive token generation generates 1 token per sequence. In each iteration step, the GPU must stream all model weights from DRAM plus the accumulated Key-Value tensors across the active batch \(B\):

\[T_{\text{decode}}(B, L_{\text{total}}) = T_{\text{launch}} + \frac{P \cdot \text{dtype\_bytes} + L_{\text{total}} \cdot D_{\text{kv\_token}}}{\text{DRAM Bandwidth (bytes/s)}}\]

Where \(D_{\text{kv\_token}}\) is the bytes per token across all layers: $\(D_{\text{kv\_token}} = 2 \times N_{\text{layers}} \times N_{\text{kv\_heads}} \times D_{\text{head}} \times \text{dtype\_bytes}\)$

docs.title: 2. Prefill-Decode Disaggregation (PD Split) Networking
docs.text:
In disaggregated serving (DistServe, Splitwise), prefill workers stream finished KV-caches to decode workers over high-speed interconnects (PCIe Gen4/5, NVLink, 100GbE):

\[T_{\text{transfer}} = \frac{L_{\text{prompt}} \cdot D_{\text{kv\_token}}}{\text{Interconnect Bandwidth (bytes/s)}} + \text{Latency}_{\text{network}}\]

When network bandwidth is sufficiently high (e.g. 100–400 Gbps), transfer latency is a negligible fraction of decode time, completely isolating decode streams from prefill latency spikes.

docs.title: 3. Queueing Dynamics (\(M/G/1\) Queues)
docs.text:
In an idealized serving system with Poisson arrivals (rate \(\lambda\)) and general service distribution \(S\), the expected waiting time in queue \(W_q\) is given by the Pollaczek–Khinchine (P-K) formula:

\[W_q = \frac{\lambda \cdot \mathbb{E}[S^2]}{2(1 - \rho)}\]

Where: * \(\rho = \lambda \cdot \mathbb{E}[S]\) is the cluster utilization. * \(\mathbb{E}[S^2] = \text{Var}(S) + (\mathbb{E}[S])^2\) represents the second moment of service time.

docs.title: Why Variance Kills Latency:
docs.text:
In asymmetric workloads (such as RAG, where prompt lengths range from 50 to 5,000 tokens), the variance \(\text{Var}(S)\) is enormous. The P-K formula proves that high variance in service time explodes waiting time \(W_q\) even when average utilization \(\rho\) is moderate!

Chunked Prefill directly dampens \(\text{Var}(S)\) by enforcing uniform chunk execution steps, driving queue waiting times down dramatically.
